context.title: Software Testing

citationSources.text: Course plan
Study chapter 1 this week, chapter 2 next week, then take the mock exam on 20 May.
Testing shows the presence of defects
Testing can show that defects are present, but cannot prove that there are none.
Exhaustive testing is impossible
Testing every combination of inputs is not feasible except in trivial cases; risk and priorities focus the effort.
Early testing saves time and money
Defects removed early, for example by reviewing requirements, cost far less to fix than defects found late.
Defects cluster together
A small number of modules usually contains most of the defects found before release.
Static testing
Static testing examines work products such as requirements and code without executing them, for example in reviews.
Dynamic testing
Dynamic testing executes the software and compares actual with expected results.
Test levels
Component, integration, system and acceptance testing, each with its own objectives.

citationSources.text: Testing principles help testers plan their work. Testing shows the presence of defects but cannot prove their absence. Exhaustive testing is impossible except in trivial cases, so risk analysis and priorities focus the effort. Early testing saves time and money because defects found in requirements cost far less to fix than defects found in production. Defects cluster together: a small number of modules usually contains most defects. Repeating the same tests finds fewer new defects over time, so tests must be reviewed and revised. Testing is context dependent: safety-critical software is tested differently from a mobile game. Finally, the absence of defects is a fallacy if the system does not meet users' needs.

messages.content: Break this card into atomic idea cards that replace it, so it is easier to digest and the connections between ideas are visible. Use cards and connections only; leave mindmap empty. Each card holds exactly one idea and makes sense on its own: a short title that states the point as a claim (for example "Early testing is cheaper", not "Early testing"), then at most about 60 words of formatted detail, with lists or a table only when they help. Keep every fact, number, example, exception and qualification from the source in some card, because the original card is removed; never add facts the source does not state. Prefer 5 to 12 cards, at most 20. Connect related cards with directional arrows labelled with exactly one of: leads to, causes, requires, part of, example of, contrasts with. The arrow points from the card the label describes, for example A requires B, A is an example of B, A is part of B. Only connect ideas the source relates; do not invent relationships. When the canvas map lists other cards whose content relates to an idea, you may link the idea card to them, never to the card being replaced.
